items.title: The earliest Christians thought Jesus would return within their lifetime
items.claim: Paul's letters (50s CE) are the oldest Christian texts. What does he tell his churches about the timing of Christ's return?

options.text: He explicitly warns that it will be many centuries away
He tells believers — in 1 Thessalonians 4 and 1 Corinthians 15 — that 'we who are alive, who are left' will be caught up to meet the Lord
He refuses to discuss the timing at all
He places the return precisely at AD 70, the destruction of the Temple

items.reveal:
1 Thessalonians 4:15-17, written around 50-51 CE, includes Paul among those still alive at the Parousia. 1 Corinthians 7:29 says 'the appointed time has grown short.' Mark 9:1 has Jesus saying 'some standing here will not taste death' before seeing the Kingdom.

When Christ did not return, later texts (e.g. 2 Peter 3:8 — 'one day is with the Lord as a thousand years') reinterpret the delay. This shift is one of the central transformations of early Christian theology.
items.why: Treating the New Testament as a unified, settled doctrine misses that it documents a community reinterpreting itself in real time. The 'delay of the Parousia' is one of the formative pressures on Christian thought.

items.title: The Four Noble Truths are framed like a medical diagnosis
items.claim: What are the Four Noble Truths of Buddhism?

options.text: Dukkha (suffering exists), Samudaya (its cause is craving/tanha), Nirodha (it can cease), Magga (the path — the Eightfold Path)
Right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort

items.reveal:
The Buddha taught the Four Noble Truths in his first sermon (Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta) at Sarnath, near Varanasi, after his enlightenment. They are structured as a medical diagnosis: symptom, cause, prognosis, treatment.

'Dukkha' is often translated 'suffering' but covers unsatisfactoriness — the inability of conditioned things to give lasting peace. 'Tanha' is craving, including for existence and non-existence.

The Eightfold Path is grouped into wisdom (right view, right intention), ethical conduct (right speech, action, livelihood) and mental discipline (right effort, mindfulness, concentration).
items.why: Buddhism is often summarised as 'life is suffering' — a misleading reduction. The Four Noble Truths are a structured argument from problem to solution, not a pessimistic mood.

items.title: Vedantic Hinduism teaches the unity of atman and Brahman

options.text: Soul and god are entirely separate

'That thou art' (Chandogya Upanishad 6.8.7) — atman (the individual self) is identical with, or in relation to, Brahman (ultimate reality); different Vedanta schools interpret the relationship as non-dual, qualified non-dual, or dualist
Only Brahman is real; atman is illusion with no relation
Brahman is a god subordinate to atman

items.reveal:
The Mahavakyas ('great sayings') include 'tat tvam asi' (Chandogya 6.8.7), 'aham brahmasmi' (Brihadaranyaka 1.4.10), 'ayam atma brahma' (Mandukya 2).

Shankara (8th century CE) developed Advaita Vedanta — non-duality: atman is identical to Brahman; perceived multiplicity is maya (illusion).

Ramanuja (11th-12th century) taught Vishishtadvaita — qualified non-duality: atman is a real attribute of Brahman but distinct. Madhva (13th century) taught Dvaita — full dualism: souls and God are eternally distinct.

All three schools are orthodox Vedantic positions.
items.why: Hindu philosophy of self is sophisticated. Treating Hinduism as 'just polytheism' misses the metaphysical core that has shaped Indian thought for over two millennia.
